title: What Makes Notre-Dame Cathedral a Masterpiece of Gothic Architecture

body:
in Architecture, History |   	November 20th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Most of us remem­ber where we were when we heard that Notre-Dame had burned down. And even upon learn­ing that the most famous of all French cathe­drals had been bad­ly dam­aged rather than com­plete­ly destroyed, it still felt as if some­thing irre­place­able had been lost. It made no dif­fer­ence whether we’d actu­al­ly been to the place, as I had­n’t at the time. When I did final­ly make it to Paris four years lat­er, Notre-Dame’s restora­tion was still under­way, and con­struc­tion walls pre­vent­ed any­one from see­ing much of any­thing at ground lev­el, let alone enter­ing. Yet crowds still gath­ered to take pic­tures in the square out­side, appar­ent­ly find­ing that prox­im­i­ty to such a civ­i­liza­tion­al land­mark was enough, even in its par­tial­ly ruined and inac­ces­si­ble state.
Even with­out a chance to step inside, expe­ri­enc­ing Notre-Dame’s sur­round­ings on the Île de la Cité, as well as the greater urban con­text of Paris, cer­tain­ly deep­ens one’s under­stand­ing of the beau­ty of the cathe­dral itself. So does vis­it­ing oth­er, less wide­ly known exam­ples of the form, as shown by archi­tec­ture-and-his­to­ry YouTu­ber Manuel Bra­vo in his new video above.
Ordi­nary tourists in Paris may make a bee­line for Notre-Dame, but they’re hard­ly like­ly to find their way out to the oth­er medieval cathe­drals in Saint-Denis, north of the city, much less all the way out in Laon. Though glo­ri­ous in their own way, they’re per­haps even more valu­able in pro­vid­ing the con­text of Goth­ic church archi­tec­ture in which Notre-Dame made such a mark.
As Bra­vo explains it, Notre-Dame’s façade rep­re­sents “the moment in which Goth­ic façade achieves its most bal­anced syn­the­sis. The exper­i­ments and inno­va­tions of Saint-Denis and Laon are absorbed, dis­ci­plined, and uni­fied into a com­po­si­tion in which no ele­ment appears arbi­trary or inde­pen­dent from the whole.” Among its most influ­en­tial appre­ci­a­tors was Vic­tor Hugo, in whose time much of Paris’ Goth­ic archi­tec­ture was being demol­ished. His roman­tic evo­ca­tions of the medieval built envi­ron­ment in Notre-Dame de Paris (in Eng­lish, The Hunch­back of Notre-Dame) helped save the much dete­ri­o­rat­ed tit­u­lar struc­ture, which received an ambi­tious ren­o­va­tion under Eugène Vio­l­let-le-Duc between 1844 and 1864. That project went beyond peri­od accu­ra­cy, adding such non-orig­i­nal details as the gallery of chimeras perched high enough to remain vis­i­ble dur­ing the lat­est restora­tion work. Vis­i­tors today may notice that the inte­ri­or does­n’t look exact­ly like it used to, but some will appre­ci­ate that even a mon­u­ment like Notre-Dame must change with the cen­turies.

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: Dramatic Waves Crash on Iceland's Coast in Photos by Vilhelm Gunnarsson
description:
All images © Vilhelm Gunnarsson, shared with permission
November 20, 2026


Along the rugged volcanic coast of Iceland’s Reykjanes Peninsula, Vilhelm
body:
All images © Vilhelm Gunnarsson, shared with permission
November 20, 2026


Along the rugged volcanic coast of Iceland’s Reykjanes Peninsula, Vilhelm Gunnarsson captures striking storm surf amid natural contrasts. Dark rocks and beaches send foamy waves into high definition, highlighting the forces that physically shape the artist’s home country. Using black-and-white, an approach inspired by fellow artist Ragnar Axelsson, Gunnarsson emphasizes profound tonal shifts and incredible vistas.
Doubling as a press photographer and a member of a local rescue team, Gunnarsson is accustomed to working in a range of conditions. He captured these images during or just after a storm, when the waves are at their highest. Once you see an otherworldly face emerging from one of the crests, which the photographer describes as a ghost, you won’t be able to unsee it. Explore a larger archive on Instagram.

title: Elegance Flows Through Sheena Liam's Embroideries in Green
description: Model and ballet dancer Sheena Liam brings her understanding of poise, elegance, and graceful bodily movements to a more fixed medium. For the pas
body:
Model and ballet dancer Sheena Liam brings her understanding of poise, elegance, and graceful bodily movements to a more fixed medium. For the past several years, the artist has been stitching tender portraits of women with long, three-dimensional braids that cascade off the fabric. Occasionally, a single loose thread appears to have slipped out of its plait as it drifts across a protagonist’s cheek.
Liam’s latest works are on view this month in her solo exhibition, The Unbearable Lightness. Several pieces feature figures sporting the same striped bodysuit with an open back, and the methodical pattern on the garment evokes both a sense of precision and rhythm depicted in the scenes. Dancers grasp hands in a circle, clutch each other at the waist, and quietly stretch in solitude, their movements steady and self-determined.

Created across the last eight years, this body of work extends Liam’s interest in women’s labor and how the slow, careful process of stitching can also be an act of defiance in an increasingly digital, fast-paced world. Each piece begins with an underlying sketch that the artist then covers in thread and typically finishes with sleek braids and quick snips of the remaining loose ends.
The Unbearable Lightness opens today at Item Gallery in Paris and runs through December 19. Follow Liam’s latest on Instagram.

body:
Community
                “I love that my roommate’s cat, Astrid, whom I appointed as my studio assistant, can always come and join me when I am painting.”
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Welcome to the 364th installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Rei Xiao paints a world of surreal, feline figuration into being while navigating the artist visa system and managing their studio assistant (a dignified cat named Astrid).Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.Rei Xiao, Brooklyn, New YorkHow long have you been working in this space?Two years.Describe an average day in your studio.I work from my apartment. The most predictable parts of my studio day start with putting on my sunscreen and painting clothes. It’s a very small space that I paint in, so I usually have to push stuff aside when I start, like my painting cart, stool, and trash bin. I, then, turn on my air purifier, open the lids of my palettes, scrape paints from the previous session, and play either TV shows I’m familiar with or podcasts hosted by comedians in the background. The day usually ends with my cleaning the palette, emptying and wiping my brush cleaning tank, and diligently washing my brushes. Then I wash my face and go to sleep.

title: The Real Miami Museums and Artists Behind GTA VI’s Vice City
description:
News
                From The Bass in Miami Beach to the murals of Wynwood, the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is heavily insp
body:
News
                From The Bass in Miami Beach to the murals of Wynwood, the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is heavily inspired by the local arts scene.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Grand Theft Auto VI protagonist Jason Duval photographed outside of the game's Vice Museum of Art, which is directly modeled after the Bass Museum of Art in Miami Beach (image courtesy David Herrera, @david.her.rera)
    
        
            After 13 agonizing years of waiting for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6), gamers worldwide wasted no time tearing up the streets of the game's fictional state of Leonida after it was released yesterday, November 19. The South Florida-inspired game environment is heavily influenced by the culture, environment, and architecture of Miami — from its Art Deco resorts, white-sand beaches, Cuban quarter, and strip clubs, right down to its museums and arts venues.As fans embed themselves in GTA 6's immersive landscape, many have recognized real-life locations across South Florida making unexpected cameos. One such case is the Vice Museum of Art, which Rockstar Games confirmed is modeled after the Bass Museum of Art in Miami Beach. “It was totally unexpected to see Grand Theft Auto VI reimagine The Bass as the ‘Vice City Museum of Art,’” said Silvia Karman Cubiñá, executive director of the Bass Museum of Art, in an email to Hyperallergic.  “It’s a wonderful reminder of how art and architecture can become part of popular culture,” she continued. “Now, I’m just curious: will the Vice City Museum of Art get more visitors than we do?!” An exterior view of the Bass Museum of Art in Miami Beach, Florida, shows the clear resemblance to the Vice Museum of Art. (photo Robin Hill, courtesy Bass Museum of Art)While not listed as a landmark like the Vice Museum of Art, another building in Downtown Vice City appears to be directly modeled after the Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM). Situated near the Vice City Arts Center, which is heavily based on Miami's Adrienne Arsht Center for Performing Arts, the PAMM-inspired building sits right on the water's edge just as the museum does in real life. “We were as delighted as anyone else to find PAMM in what feels like the biggest video game of all time,” said Alexa Ferra, PAMM's senior director of marketing and communications, in an email to Hyperallergic. Ferra attached a photo someone sent her from the game showing the PAMM dupe and some gummy bear-inspired sculptures installed in the shallow water. “It's a testament to our stunning Herzog & de Meuron building, and goes to show if you stick around long enough, you'll pop up in the unlikeliest — but inevitable — of places.” Ferra added. A view of the Pérez Art Museum Miami-inspired building and an installation of supersized gummy bear sculptures in the water off the coast of Downtown Vice City (image shared by Alexa Ferra)Other references to Miami's arts and culture scene include Leonida's Stockyard neighborhood, which directly channels the street murals and warehouse-lined roads of the Wynwood Arts District. It was reported earlier this summer that Rockstar Games had hired over 50 real street artists to design the in-game murals across Stockyard. Users shared they've spotted the works of street artist Ahol Sniffs Glue (David Anasagasti), among others.Josh Aronson, “Spring” (2024) archival pigment print (© the artist; photo by and courtesy Josh Aronson)Miami-raised contemporary photographer Josh Aronson also took notice of GTA 6's inclusion of his installation at the Catalina Hotel & Beach Club in Miami Beach during Miami Art Week 2024, which Rockstar Games incorporated in Vice City's own Catalina Hotel. From Aronson's Florida Boys (2020–) photo series, the photo “Spring” (2024) was made into an enormous sublimated fabric print that hung from the second-story window of the hotel. Josh Aronson posted about the representation of his artwork in GTA 6 on his Instagram story. (screenshot Hyperallergic via Instagram)The same printed photo, which features a group of cheerful young men photographed from above while floating in water, is shown at Vice City's Catalina Hotel.“Florida Boys is my own imagined version of Florida, so I love that it gets to live on in another imagined Florida,” Aronson told Hyperallergic. “The installation at the Catalina was temporary, but in Vice City, someone might stumble upon it years from now. It’s a reminder of the wild ways we encounter art today, and how a work can find new life long after it comes down.” GTA6's pre-holiday release comes just before Miami Art Week begins early next month. Those dropping in can find some of Aronson's installations on view beyond Vice City at the Vizcaya Museum and Gardens and the Museum of Contemporary Art, North Miami, and also pay homage to the cultural venues and districts that inspired Leonida. Who says you can't deal drugs, steal cars, kick ass, and enjoy your local arts institution? (image courtesy David Herrera, @david.her.rera)

title: Hilma af Klint Is Rolling in Her Grave
description:
Daily Newsletter
                The Swedish artist’s painting went under the hammer for an obscene amount of money. Plus: Lower
body:
Daily Newsletter
                The Swedish artist’s painting went under the hammer for an obscene amount of money. Plus: Lowery Stokes Sims reviews Richard Powell’s new book on pigment, Blackness, and paint.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Nothing in visual culture is neutral, least of all the color wheel itself. Scholar Richard Powell explores this deceptively simple truth in his new book, tackling the theoretical entanglement of race and pigment and how Black painters have used color over time. Trailblazing art historian Lowery Stokes Sims, formerly a curator at the Met Museum and director of the Studio Museum in Harlem, parses his richly layered essays today, linking the critical theory of Josef Albers and Darby English to the practices of artists like Jacob Lawrence and Alma Thomas. The book, Sims writes, shifted the way she’ll look at art moving forward.Meanwhile, on the other end of the spectrum: News broke that a 1920 painting by Hilma af Klint sold for $12.7 million. Yes, the same Hilma af Klint who described herself less as an artist and more as a channel for a higher power, who followed the guidance of spirits that took physical form through her paintings. But hey, at least the painting’s owner has a new addition to their investment portfolio?In reviews, Alina Cohen spends time with the poignant, impactful photographs by Laia Abril, who evokes the systems of patriarchy and sexual violence through the quietly haunting garments and objects in their wake. As the Cornell 7 case continues and convicted abusers sit in office, Abril’s photographs “reject both the invisibility of some crimes and the all-too-visible nature of others.” More, as always, below.—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books

	
		
			Richard Powell Unsettles Race and Color Theory
		
	
	
		I was aware of the place of color theory in the practice of art and knew the names of important theorists, from Johann Wolfgang von Goethe to Johannes Itten to Josef Albers. But otherwise, I presumed artists’ palettes were the result of personal predilection, technical explorations (i.e., the opening up of brushstrokes and form in the 19th century and the introduction of a wall of color in the 20th century), or cultural orientation. So it was therefore with great interest that I approached reading Richard Powell’s latest publication, Colorstruck!: Painting, Pigment, Affect  (2026). | Lowery Stokes Sims
